source: Lai, Robbins (1985) Asymptotically efficient adaptive allocation rules (as restated in Auer 2002 and Bubeck 2012)
finding: Founding lower bound. Any consistent policy must play each suboptimal arm at least about ln(n) / KL times. So regret must grow at least logarithmically. Their index policies reach this, but are hard to compute.
numbers: E[T_j(n)] >= (1/D(p_j||p*) + o(1)) ln n, where D is the KL divergence between arm j and the best arm.
limits: Original 1985 paper NOT opened; read only as restated in two later papers. Holds for regular one-parameter reward families.
agent_relevance: Tells us what the best possible exploration cost is: with 8 operators the cost of finding the best one is at least log in the number of trials, never zero.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem
finding: UCB1: play the arm with highest (mean reward + sqrt(2 ln n / n_i)). First simple policy with logarithmic regret uniformly over time (not only in the limit), for any rewards in [0,1], no prior knowledge needed.
numbers: Theorem 1: expected regret after n plays <= 8 * sum over suboptimal i of (ln n / Delta_i) + (1 + pi^2/3) * sum of Delta_j.
quote: the optimal logarithmic regret is also achievable uniformly over time
limits: Constant 8/Delta^2 is worse than Lai-Robbins 1/KL, because KL >= 2*Delta^2 (so best possible constant here is 1/(2 Delta^2)). The bound is a worst-over-time bound and is loose at small n.
agent_relevance: Default deterministic selector over operators. Needs rewards scaled to [0,1] and many pulls per arm before the confidence term shrinks.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem
finding: Real experiments on Bernoulli arms: UCB1-Tuned (variance-aware index, min{1/4, V_j + sqrt(2 ln t / s)}) beats plain UCB1 in essentially all cases, but has no proof. UCB2 is similar to UCB1-Tuned but always slightly worse, and not sensitive to its alpha parameter (0.001 used).
limits: Run lengths of 100,000 plays are far beyond what an agent with a few dozen trials per task can afford. Tuned index chosen after looking at the same kind of settings.
agent_relevance: If we use UCB, use a variance-aware index. Theory-safe UCB1 over-explores at small budgets.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem
finding: epsilon_n-greedy (explore with probability c*K/(d^2 n), decaying) is the baseline. Well tuned it performs almost always best. But it needs the gap d between best and second-best arm, and mistuning degrades it fast. It is worst when there are many bad arms (distributions 12 and 14), since it explores uniformly.
numbers: No single value of c worked on all 7 settings; the authors searched c per setting. Unfair advantage to e-greedy in the plots.
limits: Tuned-per-setting result; with an untuned c, e-greedy lost. The result says tuning is the hidden cost, not that e-greedy is better.
agent_relevance: A fixed-order or random fallback is a strong baseline when few operators are bad; bandits only win clearly when many operators are bad or when tuning is not possible.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem
finding: UCB1-Normal for Gaussian rewards with unknown mean and variance. Regret is still logarithmic, but the proof depends on two tail-bound conjectures checked only numerically.
numbers: Theorem 4 bound: 256 (log n) * sum of sigma_i^2/Delta_i + (1 + pi^2/2 + 8 log n) * sum of Delta_j (as extracted from the PDF text; formula garbled by extraction).
limits: Not fully proved. Constants are huge (256).
agent_relevance: Operator rewards are rarely bounded Bernoulli; this is the nearest principled option for continuous gains, but its constants make it useless at small n.

source: Agrawal, Goyal (2012) Analysis of Thompson Sampling for the multi-armed bandit problem
finding: First logarithmic regret bound for Thompson sampling (TS), a 1933 Bayesian heuristic: sample a mean for each arm from its Beta posterior, play the arm with the largest sample. The analysis is prior-free (works for fixed unknown arm means), and extends to rewards in [0,1].
numbers: Two arms: E[R(T)] = O(ln T / Delta + 1/Delta^3). N arms: O((sum_{a>=2} 1/Delta_a^2)^2 ln T). Compare UCB1: 8 sum ln T / Delta_a. TS algorithm starts from Beta(1,1) for each arm.
limits: Dependence on gaps is worse than UCB1 (square of the sum, versus linear in 1/Delta). Not yet asymptotically optimal. They cite earlier empirical reports that TS handles delayed or batched feedback better than UCB.
agent_relevance: TS needs no confidence-bound tuning: only a prior. This is the cheapest bandit to implement with 8 operators and binary pass/fail credit.

source: Kaufmann, Korda, Munos (2012) Thompson Sampling: an asymptotically optimal finite time analysis
finding: Thompson sampling with Beta(1,1) priors on Bernoulli rewards is asymptotically optimal: it matches the Lai-Robbins lower bound. Closes a question open since 1933. Analysis links a TS sample to the Bayes-UCB posterior quantile.
numbers: Theorem 1: for every eps>0, R(T) <= (1+eps) * sum over suboptimal a of Delta_a (ln T + ln ln T) / KL(mu_a, mu*) + C(eps, mu_1..mu_K).
limits: Bernoulli rewards only. Constant C depends on the problem and can be large, so it says nothing about regret at T = 30.
agent_relevance: Gives a principled reason to prefer TS over UCB for pass/fail operator credit: same asymptotic rate as the best possible.

source: Kaufmann, Korda, Munos (2012) Thompson Sampling: an asymptotically optimal finite time analysis
finding: Simulations show TS beating the other asymptotically optimal policies. All optimal policies beat UCB even at small horizons. TS is also the easiest to implement: one posterior sample per arm instead of an optimisation (KL-UCB) or quantile (Bayes-UCB).
numbers: Two-arm test, T=10,000, mu=(0.2,0.25) and (0.8,0.9), averaged over N=20,000 runs: TS always beat KL-UCB and beat Bayes-UCB at large horizons. 10-arm test, T=20,000, N=50,000 runs, mu=(0.1,0.05,0.05,0.05,0.02,0.02,0.02,0.01,0.01,0.01): TS best of the optimal policies.
limits: Authors say curves are from figures; exact regret values not in text. Horizons of 10^4 or more.
agent_relevance: At T near 10^4 TS wins; our T is two to three orders smaller, so this is no proof it wins for us.

source: Chapelle, Li (2011) An empirical evaluation of Thompson sampling
finding: Broad empirical case for Thompson sampling: simulated Bernoulli bandits, display advertising, and Yahoo news recommendation. TS is competitive or better than UCB and epsilon-greedy, has no parameter to tune, and degrades less when feedback is delayed. Authors argue TS should be a standard baseline.
numbers: Simulation: K in {10,100}, epsilon-gap in {0.02,0.1}, averaged over 100 repetitions, Beta(1,1) prior. News data: 34M randomized serving events, 7 days in June 2009, offline unbiased evaluation, delays 10, 30, 60 min.
quote: it should be part of the standard baselines to compare against
limits: Figure values were not in the extracted text; regret numbers for the main simulations not recorded. Industrial settings have huge sample sizes.
agent_relevance: TS needs no tuning parameter, which matters when we cannot afford to tune the selector on few trials.

source: Chapelle, Li (2011) An empirical evaluation of Thompson sampling
finding: Delayed feedback hurts the deterministic UCB much more than randomized TS. With a dynamic set of 10 items, regret ratio UCB/TS grows from 2.65 (no delay) to 3.82 (delay 1000).
limits: Synthetic. Authors give the reason as randomization avoiding repeated bad choices during the delay; not tested directly.
agent_relevance: If our agent runs operators in parallel batches and sees the outcome only after the batch, use a randomized selector (TS), not UCB.

source: Chapelle, Li (2011) An empirical evaluation of Thompson sampling
finding: Making the Beta posterior narrower (dividing both Beta parameters by alpha, with alpha<1, so less exploration) can lower regret in the non-asymptotic regime. In display ads, alpha=0.5 was slightly better than standard TS (alpha=1). Exploit-only did well versus random, and epsilon-greedy did not beat exploit-only, because context changes force implicit exploration. Posterior variance was well calibrated: 95% interval contained the true CTR 95.1% of the time.
numbers: Display ads table: TS best regret; alpha=0.5 slightly better than alpha=1. Figure 3 setting: K=10 lower-left of Fig 1, 1000 repetitions, T up to 10^7.
limits: Direction of the posterior change inferred from the text 'parameters divided by alpha' and 'alpha<1 yielded better regrets'. Gain is small and reduces asymptotic guarantees.
agent_relevance: At small budgets, less exploration than textbook TS is often better. Treat the prior strength as a tunable, and test it in simulation first.

source: Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband, Wen (2018) A tutorial on Thompson sampling
finding: TS is probability matching: each arm is chosen with the posterior probability that it is the best. It explores only where information could change the best arm, and does not waste trials on arms almost surely worse. Greedy selection can lock onto a poor arm forever.
numbers: Three-arm Beta-Bernoulli, theta=(0.9,0.8,0.7), uniform prior, 10,000 simulations of 1,000 periods: greedy does not always converge to arm 1, TS does, and TS per-period regret vanishes. In the worked posterior example TS picks arms 1,2,3 with probabilities ~0.82, 0, 0.18.
limits: Tutorial simulations, 1000 periods, not tiny budgets. Greedy lock-in depends on tie-breaking and priors.
agent_relevance: Direct support for 'do not just exploit the first operator that worked': a greedy operator picker locks in. Probability matching spends trials where the answer could change.

source: Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband, Wen (2018) A tutorial on Thompson sampling
finding: Prior matters. Using an informative, correct ('coherent') prior cuts regret versus a uniform prior that does not match the world, and a wrong prior delays learning.
numbers: Three-arm Bernoulli bandit, mean rewards drawn from beta(1,50), beta(1,100), beta(1,200); average over 10,000 simulations; coherent prior gives lower regret than uniform (misspecified) prior.
limits: Simulated; one setting. Shows direction, not size, in the text we read.
agent_relevance: A prior borrowed from other problem classes (our SUBFIELDS question) can speed learning if right, and slow it if wrong. Needs a check on held-out classes.

source: Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband, Wen (2018) A tutorial on Thompson sampling
finding: Nonstationary TS: inject uncertainty every step (decay toward the prior) so beliefs stay wide. Plain TS, which treats rewards as constant, degrades as the arms drift. No algorithm keeps regret going to zero when the world drifts.
numbers: Nonstationary Bernoulli bandit, prior alpha=beta=1, decay rate gamma=0.01, 10,000 simulations per point; nonstationary TS keeps 'reasonable performance', plain TS 'becomes less effective'.
limits: Single drift model. Value of gamma chosen to match the generating process, which an agent will not know.
agent_relevance: Operator usefulness changes as the solving state changes (S3 vs S5 vs S6). Condition the bandit on state, or use forgetting.

source: Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband, Wen (2018) A tutorial on Thompson sampling
finding: When arms share structure (shortest-path edges with correlated delays), TS that models the correlation ('coherent') clearly beats TS that treats arms as independent ('misspecified').
numbers: Binomial bridge shortest path, mu_e = -1/2, sigma_e^2 = 1, 10,000 simulations per point (Fig. 7).
limits: Combinatorial path problem, not operator choice. Result concerns modelling, not the sampling rule.
agent_relevance: Our operators are correlated (G4: samples from one model are not independent). Independent-arm bandits will double count evidence.

source: Garivier, Moulines (2008/2011) On upper-confidence bound policies for non-stationary bandit problems
finding: UCB for abruptly changing rewards. Two fixes: discounted UCB (D-UCB, weight older rewards by gamma<1) and sliding-window UCB (SW-UCB, use only the last tau plays). Both lose only a log factor against the lower bound. With no breakpoints, the best window is the full horizon, i.e. standard UCB.
numbers: With Upsilon_T breakpoints in T rounds, tuning tau = 2B sqrt(T log T / Upsilon_T) gives E[N~_T(i)] = O(sqrt(T Upsilon_T log T)). Theorem 13: lower bound of order sqrt(T) for abrupt changes (stated in the paper). If breakpoints are dense (rate r), window must stay bounded away from T.
limits: Needs the number of breakpoints (or a rate) to tune the window. Regret is sublinear only if breakpoints are sparse.
agent_relevance: Defines the price of nonstationarity: windows of about sqrt(T) pulls. For T = 30 per class there is almost nothing to adapt.

source: Garivier, Moulines (2008/2011) On upper-confidence bound policies for non-stationary bandit problems
finding: Simulation: D-UCB and SW-UCB find the changes quickly; plain UCB1 stays on the old best arm for a very long time after the second break, though it reacts fast to the first break (loose confidence interval at that moment). EXP3.S is also slower.
numbers: 3 arms (Bernoulli), arm 3 has p=0.4 except p=0.9 for 3000<=t<5000. Parameters: UCB1 xi=1/2; D-UCB xi=1/2, gamma=1-1/(4 sqrt T); SW-UCB tau=4 sqrt(T log T); EXP3.S per Auer Cor 8.3. Second test, 2 arms, p1=0.5+0.4cos(6 pi t/T), p2=0.5.
limits: Parameters tuned to horizon and number of breaks. Only qualitative results from figures; T not recovered from text.
agent_relevance: Confirms: a stationary UCB trusts old evidence too long. Forgetting is needed once the world changes at unknown times.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund, Schapire (2002) The nonstochastic multiarmed bandit problem
finding: EXP3: bandit algorithm for adversarial rewards using exponential weights and importance-weighted reward estimates. No assumption that rewards are random. Exp3.S adds a switching comparator: regret against the best sequence of S switches.
numbers: Cor 3.2: with g >= best total reward and gamma = min(1, sqrt(K ln K / ((e-1) g))), weak regret <= 2 sqrt(e-1) sqrt(g K ln K) ~ 2.63 sqrt(g K ln K). Cor 8.3: Exp3.S regret <= 2 sqrt(e-1) sqrt(K T (S ln(KT) + e)) with alpha=1/T.
limits: Bounds are worst-case and larger than stochastic bounds. Importance weights make estimates noisy at small T.
agent_relevance: Safe option when operator outcomes may be adversarial or depend on our own earlier moves; costs speed.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Freund, Schapire (2002) The nonstochastic multiarmed bandit problem
finding: Matching lower bound: no algorithm beats about sqrt(K T) regret in the adversarial model. So EXP3 is optimal up to log factors; the gap between stochastic (log T) and adversarial (sqrt T) settings is real.
numbers: Theorem 5.1: for any K>=2 and horizon T, there is a reward distribution with expected weak regret >= (1/20) min{ sqrt(K T), T }.
limits: Only worst-case. Real operator rewards are neither fully adversarial nor fully stochastic.
agent_relevance: With K=8 operators and T<~64 trials regret bound min(sqrt(KT),T) is almost T: nothing can be proven to learn at that scale; any gain must come from priors.

source: Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi (2012) Regret analysis of stochastic and nonstochastic multi-armed bandit problems
finding: Survey: gap-dependent regret is logarithmic (UCB, Lai-Robbins), but the minimax (worst-gap) rate is sqrt(nK). MOSS removes the extra log factor. TS has been analysed with a frequentist view and matches the UCB-type bound, per Agrawal-Goyal and Kaufmann et al.
numbers: Minimax lower bound of order sqrt(nK); UCB regret <= sqrt(nK ln n) up to a constant; MOSS <= min{sqrt(nK), (K/Delta) ln(n Delta^2/K)} up to a constant.
limits: Survey, not new experiments.
agent_relevance: Use this survey as the formal reference. The sqrt(nK) bound says small-gap operators cannot be told apart at small n.

source: Da Costa, Fialho, Schoenauer, Sebag (2008) Adaptive operator selection with dynamic multi-armed bandits
finding: Dynamic MAB (D-MAB) for adaptive operator selection (AOS) in evolutionary algorithms: run UCB1 and restart all counts when a Page-Hinkley change test fires. Also UCB with reward scaling, since UCB's exploration term assumes rewards in [0,1] but EA gains are not. Two scalings: multiplicative (fixed factor S) and affine (rescale to give the best operator a fixed selection pressure).
numbers: Page-Hinkley: tolerance delta=0.15, threshold gamma in [0.5,10] (uniform scenario) or [10,20]; restart = set n_i, mean, m_i, M_i to 0 for all arms. Restart judged more robust than discounting.
limits: Several parameters (delta, gamma, scaling S): 2 more than static MAB. Authors admit automatic setting is future work.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete recipe: credit assignment (reward + scaling) then decision rule (UCB or TS). Restarting on a change signal fits G1 (act only on a signal).

source: Da Costa, Fialho, Schoenauer, Sebag (2008) Adaptive operator selection with dynamic multi-armed bandits
finding: Test bed: K=5 operators; rewards fixed within an epoch, then permuted among operators; 10 epochs, epoch length T=50 or 200. Three reward laws: Uniform (best on [4,6], second [3,5] ... worst [0,2]), Boolean (0 or 10; best has prob .5, then .4, ...), Outlier (0 w.p. .9; best gets 50 w.p. .1, next 40 ...). Measures: p_best and total cumulative reward (TCR). Each algorithm tuned by factorial design with 100 runs per setting, ANOVA and Scheffe tests.
numbers: Optimal play gets 5 per step: max TCR 2500 (T=50) and 10,000 (T=200). Compared: Probability Matching (PM), Adaptive Pursuit (AP), MAB-M, MAB-A (static UCB, multiplicative or affine), D-MAB-M, D-MAB-A.
limits: Artificial scenarios from Thierens (2005) plus two new ones; best parameters picked on the same scenarios used to report (optimistic for all methods).
agent_relevance: A cheap simulation template for testing our own selector at small budgets: permute which operator is best at unknown times.

source: Da Costa, Fialho, Schoenauer, Sebag (2008) Adaptive operator selection with dynamic multi-armed bandits
finding: Uniform scenario results: bandits beat PM and AP. Dynamic version slightly best with long epochs. At T=200 TCR: PM 7.36k, AP 9.19k, MAB-M 9.46k, MAB-A 8.18k, D-MAB-M 9.75k, D-MAB-A 9.79k (max 10k). p_best: .34, .75, .84, .47, .92, .94. At T=50 (max 2.5k): 1.80, 2.12, 2.25, 1.98, 2.24, 2.20k; static MAB-M and D-MAB-M best.
numbers: TCR in units of 1000; scores from Tables 2 and 3 of the paper, mean over 100 runs, with small standard errors (e.g. D-MAB-A 9.79 +- 0.059).
limits: Short epochs (50 pulls with 5 arms) remove the advantage of the change detector: static MAB-M equals D-MAB. Affine scaling hurt static UCB (MAB-A 8.18k) but not D-MAB.
agent_relevance: Relevant to small N: with only 10 pulls per arm per epoch, a plain UCB with good scaling is as good as the fancy detector.

source: Da Costa, Fialho, Schoenauer, Sebag (2008) Adaptive operator selection with dynamic multi-armed bandits
finding: Boolean scenario: plain static MAB-M is best; the detector does not help. Outlier scenario (rare large rewards): every method is close to random guessing, and the response surface is chaotic.
numbers: Boolean, T=200 TCR (k): PM 7.90, AP 8.13, MAB-M 8.19, MAB-A 7.50, D-MAB-M 7.57, D-MAB-A 7.71; p_best .43,.48,.52,.35,.38,.41. Outlier, T=200: TCR 6.17 to 7.12k; p_best .21 to .29 (random = .2).
limits: Outlier case is a caricature of rare big wins, yet it is the case that matters for finding breakthrough operators.
agent_relevance: Heavy-tailed rewards defeat mean-based selectors. If an operator pays off rarely but hugely (a rare insight), a bandit on mean reward will not find it.

source: Da Costa, Fialho, Schoenauer, Sebag (2008) Adaptive operator selection with dynamic multi-armed bandits
finding: Partial failure to replicate the earlier Probability Matching / Adaptive Pursuit setup of Thierens. Best p_min was 0 to 0.01, not 0.1; and in Boolean and Outlier scenarios PM and AP were not significantly different from each other. Authors read this as: when the best operator changes quickly, being greedy is fine.
numbers: Uniform scenario results agreed with the earlier PM/AP reports; the other two did not. p_min grid 0 to 0.1 step .01; alpha 0.1 to 1.
limits: Original Thierens paper not opened; only reported through this paper's text.
agent_relevance: Minimum selection probability is a key parameter. A forced floor on exploration (like our weakest-operator probes) may be a waste when changes are fast.

source: Sun, Li (2020) Adaptive operator selection based on dynamic Thompson sampling for MOEA/D
finding: Dynamic Thompson sampling (DYTS) for operator selection in MOEA/D. Each of 5 operators (four differential-evolution variants and uniform mutation) has a Beta posterior. If alpha+beta < C, update normally; otherwise rescale so alpha+beta = C. This caps the evidence and so keeps the posterior wide and forgetful. Credit = fitness improvement of the offspring.
numbers: C = 100. Pool: DE/rand/1, DE/rand/2, DE/current-to-rand/1, DE/current-to-rand/2, uniform mutation.
limits: Preprint submitted for publication (not peer reviewed in the version read). Binary Bernoulli reward is awkward for continuous fitness gain; paper's exact mapping of FI to a reward not fully recorded.
agent_relevance: A one-line change to TS (cap alpha+beta) gives forgetting. Easy to test for our 8 operators.

source: Sun, Li (2020) Adaptive operator selection based on dynamic Thompson sampling for MOEA/D
finding: MOEA/D-DYTS versus MOEA/D-DE, -FRRMAB (a UCB-based AOS), -GRA, -IRA on 19 test problems. Authors report DYTS best in 16 of 19 comparisons for IGD and 18 of 19 for HV, with Wilcoxon rank-sum at 5%.
numbers: UF1-UF10 (30 variables; N=300 for 2 objectives, 600 for 3; 300,000 evaluations) and WFG1-WFG9 (38 variables; N=100; 25,000 evaluations). C=100. Example IGD: UF6 3.04E-2 (DYTS) vs 5.26E-2 (FRRMAB); WFG2 0.406 vs 0.756 (FRRMAB).
limits: Internal inconsistency: the printed IGD table shows MOEA/D-GRA or IRA better on UF8, UF9 (and WFG1), while the text says DYTS is best on UF8 and 16 of 19. Same authors' group as the UCB-based baseline (FRRMAB). No ablation vs plain TS in what I read.
agent_relevance: Shows a bandit-selected operator pool beats a fixed operator in EC; effect sizes uncertain. Treat as weak evidence for TS over UCB.

source: Ashizawa et al. (2025) Bandit-based prompt design strategy selection improves prompt optimizers (OPTS)
finding: LLM use of Thompson sampling: pick one prompt design strategy (about eleven, such as Chain-of-Thought, role prompting, re-reading, rephrase-and-respond, shortening) plus an 'inaction' arm per candidate prompt, inside EvoPrompt. Beta priors, binary reward (1 if the new prompt's dev score beats the incumbents, else 0). The prompt-designing LLM then applies that one strategy.
numbers: Task LLMs: Llama-3-8B-Instruct and GPT-4o mini (prompt-designing LLM: GPT-4o mini). Benchmark: BIG-Bench Hard, 27 tasks (3 tasks for GPT-4o mini). 3 seeds, population 10, 50 iterations. Variants: OPTS(TS), OPTS(US) uniform choice, OPTS(APET) LLM chooses strategies itself.
quote: explicit selection mechanisms for prompt design
limits: Dev set is also used for the reward, so overfitting to dev score is possible; test set is held out. Only 3 seeds; 50 iterations x 10 prompts is a larger budget than a single problem solve.
agent_relevance: Closest published design to our case: a bandit chooses which strategy (operator) to apply, an inaction arm lets 'do nothing' win, and the program, not the model, does the choosing (matches G5).

source: Ashizawa et al. (2025) Bandit-based prompt design strategy selection improves prompt optimizers (OPTS)
finding: Results: explicit selection helps; TS is best overall; letting the LLM choose strategies itself is worse than random choice. Gains are task-dependent: huge on some tasks (ruin names ~40%, logical deduction with GPT-4o mini ~50%), small on others.
numbers: Llama-3-8B: all three OPTS variants raise EvoPrompt(DE) average by about 4.5 to 7.5% over plain EvoPrompt; OPTS(TS) beats OPTS(US) by ~1.7% and OPTS(APET) by ~2.7% on average. Example task 'ruin names' dev example: manual 18.5, EvoPrompt 31.0, APET 65.5, EvoPrompt-OPTS(TS) 70.5. GPT-4o mini task 8: EvoPrompt(DE) 2.67 vs OPTS(TS) 52.33 (sd 11.45). Paper reports a case where CoT was applied twice to the same prompt.
limits: TS advantage over uniform (~1.7%) is small next to run-to-run sd (several points) on 3 seeds; no significance test seen. Percentages may be relative or absolute points; text is ambiguous. Big gains concentrated on a few tasks where the baseline was near zero.
agent_relevance: Supports bandit-selected strategies, but the uniform-random baseline gets most of the gain. Suggests the main value is having a program pick, not which bandit rule. LLM self-selection of strategy is biased (matches G4/G5).

source: Shi, Yang, Yang, Shen (2024) Best arm identification for prompt learning under a limited budget (TRIPLE)
finding: Prompt selection under a fixed number of LLM evaluations is best-arm identification, not regret minimisation. TRIPLE uses Sequential Halving and Continuously Reject. Baselines: Uniform (equal evaluations) and vanilla UCB. Small pools of 10 prompts, budget 50, gpt-3.5: TRIPLE-CR beats Uniform on every task shown by 8 to 129% (avg 35%) and beats UCB by 3 to 30% (avg 13%).
numbers: 12 of 47 tasks (Instruction Induction, BigBench); gpt-3.5-turbo-1106 and Llama2-7b; scores normalised to Uniform; 20 independent runs per bar. Pool of 10, budget 50 (5 evaluations per prompt).
quote: The improvement over UCB further highlights the ineffectiveness of methods for regret minimization in prompt learning
limits: Reported gains are relative to a weak uniform baseline; UCB-versus-TRIPLE differences are smaller. Selection quality scored on dev data; final test accuracy used. Only 12 tasks shown in the main text.
agent_relevance: At very small budgets (5 evaluations per prompt) smart allocation beats uniform by about a third. This is the closest match to our budget.

source: Shi, Yang, Yang, Shen (2024) Best arm identification for prompt learning under a limited budget (TRIPLE)
finding: Larger pools and lower budgets: embeddings help (TRIPLE-CLST clusters prompts; TRIPLE-GSE uses function approximation). Gains over baselines shrink as the budget grows and vanish at 30 evaluations per prompt.
numbers: Pool 30, budget 150: CLST and GSE beat the best plain TRIPLE (CR) by 2 to 60%, averaging 13% and 16%. Llama2-7b: average 45% (GSE) and 51% (CLST) over Uniform; 200% on one task. Budget per prompt 10: +9.7% (CR), +13.5% (CLST), +17.4% (GSE) over Uniform; 20: ~8%; 30 (900 total): all about equal.
limits: Gain over Uniform at larger budgets is shrinking to zero by design: with enough evaluations any method finds the best prompt. Authors advise starting small and raising budget step by step.
agent_relevance: Evidence for G12 (spend by difficulty): the value of smart allocation is highest at low budget, and zero at high budget. Our setting is low budget, so it is where bandits pay.
